extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals, crisis managers, organizational leaders, and communicators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting and executing crisis communication strategies for organizations using Situational Crisis Communication Theory (SCCT). Focuses on classifying crises, attributing responsibility, and matching response tactics to protect reputation and rebuild trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis Type (victim / accidental / preventable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crises are classified into three main categories — victim, accidental, and preventable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victim crises (e.g., natural disasters, product tampering) involve little to no fault by the organization. Accidental crises (e.g., technical failures, unintentional mistakes) imply limited responsibility. Preventable crises (e.g., misconduct, negligence) place full responsibility on the organization. The crisis type guides the tone, strategy, and level of accountability required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational Reputation as a moderating variable
rubrics_metrics.description: A company’s pre-crisis reputation influences stakeholder reactions; strong credibility and transparency can buffer reputational damage, while past ethical lapses can magnify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations with a strong record of ethical behavior, transparent communication, and consistent stakeholder engagement enjoy a reputational buffer. Reputation should be considered when choosing how accommodative or defensive a response to be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis History
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated incidents or a poor crisis track record intensify stakeholder skepticism and demand more accommodative responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an organization has prior similar incidents, stakeholders expect stronger accountability (e.g., full apologies, corrective actions). Crisis history increases perceived responsibility and the severity of reputational threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of Attributed Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization’s level of responsibility for a crisis determines the severity of reputational threat and the type of communication strategy required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholder perceptions of blame (low to high) should drive whether the response is defensive, explanatory, apologetic, or reparative. Accurately assessing attribution is central to SCCT decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match response strategy to crisis attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT provides a structured method for determining how organizations should communicate during and after a crisis by connecting crisis type, level of responsibility, and response strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single approach fits all situations — organizations must match their response strategy to the crisis type and perceived responsibility to minimize harm, preserve trust, and demonstrate responsible leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deny Strategy (use when wrongly accused)
rubrics_metrics.description: Used when the organization faces false allegations or unverified claims; the goal is to protect reputation by rejecting the connection to the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions include refuting incorrect information, clarifying facts to the public and media, and shifting attention to the actual source of the issue. Example: initial denial and cooperation with authorities in the 1982 Tylenol case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminish Strategy (reduce perceived severity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeks to lessen stakeholder anger by explaining that the event’s impact or the organization’s responsibility is lower than perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions include providing context or clarification about the cause, highlighting mitigating circumstances, and emphasizing corrective steps already taken. Often used in accidental crises. Example: early explanations by Samsung during Galaxy Note 7 incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuild Strategy (apology, compensation, corrective action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Involves apologies, compensation, and corrective action; used for preventable crises or when the organization is clearly at fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions include public acknowledgment of mistakes, offering compensation or restitution, and implementing reforms with transparent follow-ups. Example: Volkswagen issuing public apologies, settlements, and reforms after the emissions scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolstering Strategy (reinforce positive reputation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive approach used alongside other strategies to remind stakeholders of the organization’s past good performance and ongoing commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions include highlighting previous achievements and CSR efforts, showing appreciation to loyal customers and employees, and framing the crisis as a temporary setback. Example: Toyota reinforcing its history of quality during recalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victim-cluster tactical guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For victim crises (low attribution of responsibility), recommended strategies focus on empathy and transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express concern for those affected, demonstrate compassion through supportive actions, and communicate ongoing corrective or preventive measures. Use sympathy responses to reinforce goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental-cluster tactical guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For accidental crises (moderate attribution of responsibility), the best approach is an explanation strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify what happened and why, share corrective steps to prevent recurrence, and communicate responsibility without over-apologizing. This preserves credibility and shows professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventable-cluster tactical guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For preventable crises (high attribution of responsibility), effective response requires humility and transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issue a sincere apology, accept accountability, disclose corrective measures and disciplinary actions, and commit to structural changes that prevent recurrence. Focus on reputation restoration through corrective communication and authentic leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation management principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation is both the most vulnerable and the most valuable asset during a crisis; the way an organization communicates, accepts responsibility, and demonstrates accountability determines recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond with authenticity, empathy, and accountability. Align messages with long-term values; use communication to transform scrutiny into an opportunity to rebuild trust and strengthen stakeholder relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for timely and transparent data
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective use of SCCT requires accurate and prompt information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependence on timely and transparent data is critical because misinformation spreads quickly in digital crises. Without accurate information, choosing and executing the right strategy is compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to social media crises
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT adapts to digital and social media environments, where responses must be immediate, transparent, and consistent across channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social platforms amplify stakeholder reactions; timely engagement, consistent messaging, and cross-channel transparency are essential for reputation protection online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: assumption of predictable audience perception
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT assumes stakeholder reactions follow predictable patterns of attribution, which may not always hold true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in emotionally charged crises or across diverse cultural contexts where attribution and forgiveness patterns vary; validate assumptions with stakeholder insight and data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: restricted usefulness in multi-crisis scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT’s linear approach may struggle when multiple crises occur simultaneously or interactively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In complex, overlapping crises (e.g., operational failures plus leadership scandals), supplement SCCT with more dynamic frameworks to account for overlapping reputational dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: focus on communication vs root causes
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT focuses on guiding response messaging but does not directly address operational or ethical issues that caused the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SCCT alongside operational fixes and accountability mechanisms; communications without real corrective action will not fully restore reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to combine SCCT with complementary frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: To overcome SCCT constraints, experts recommend combining it with frameworks like Image Restoration Theory (Benoit, 1995) or Integrated Crisis Mapping (ICM).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complementary models can address emotional, behavioral, and reputational dimensions, making the overall response more holistic and adaptive to modern crisis dynamics.
